value.overview: The Bat Falcon (Falco rufigularis) is a small, powerful falcon of tropical forests and forest edges. It is named for its ability to capture bats, especially around dusk, but small birds are an important part of its diet. With rapid wingbeats, sharp turns, and compact proportions, it resembles a miniature forest-dwelling hobby. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, usually encountered singly or in pairs in suitable lowland and foothill habitats.
value.classification: The Bat Falcon belongs to the falcon family, Falconidae, and the genus Falco. It is one of the smaller tropical falcons and is unrelated to true nightjars or other nocturnal birds despite its common name.
value.identification: Adults are dark slate-gray to black above, with a black head and a contrasting white or buff throat. The lower breast, belly, thighs, and undertail coverts are rich rufous, often with fine dark barring. The tail is dark with narrow pale bands. It has pointed wings, a relatively short tail, a hooked falcon bill, and a fast, direct flight. Juveniles are generally browner and less sharply marked. Its swift aerial behavior helps distinguish it from larger falcons.
value.rangeHabitat: The Bat Falcon ranges from Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it occurs on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, mainly from sea level through the foothills and middle elevations, although it is local and may be overlooked. It uses humid and seasonally dry forest, forest borders, river corridors, clearings, plantations with tall trees, and other semi-open areas near woodland. It often hunts from exposed perches overlooking open airspace.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and throughout most of its range. It is not a regular long-distance migrant, though individuals may make local movements in response to prey availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The Bat Falcon usually nests in cavities, including abandoned woodpecker holes and natural hollows in trees, and may also use cavities or ledges associated with cliffs or structures. It does not normally build a substantial nest. The female lays a small clutch, and both adults defend the nesting area while the female performs most incubation and the male supplies much of the food. Breeding timing varies geographically; in Costa Rica it is associated with the local dry or early wet season in many areas.
value.dietFeeding: Small birds caught in aerial pursuit are a major food source. The falcon also takes bats, particularly around dawn and dusk, as well as large flying insects and occasionally small mammals or reptiles. It commonly waits on a prominent perch, then launches after prey with rapid acceleration and tight maneuvering. It may hunt along forest edges, over clearings, beside rivers, or near buildings and other places where flying prey concentrates.
value.behavior: The Bat Falcon is agile, alert, and often inconspicuous until it suddenly launches from a high perch. It is most active during the day but may continue hunting at twilight when bats emerge. Pairs may defend territories with fast display flights and sharp calls. It usually spends long periods perched quietly, making forest edges, dead snags, utility wires, and tall isolated trees useful places for observation. It is often seen alone or with its mate rather than in flocks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently classified as threatened.
